w: What's tested The hinge-and-slide joint, its disc and its two spaces Which ligament stops which movement Each chewing muscle, its parts and its job The exam chart of muscles for each jaw movement The muscles above and below the hyoid bone This lecture is anatomy for dentists: how the jaw parts work, not every bump on the bone. Dr. Givan won't ask about nerves or blood supply. The jaw joint Dogs hinge, cows grind, and we do both. The jaw joint hinges like an elbow and slides like a wrist, so it's called ginglymoarthrodial. Both joints belong to one bone, so one side can't move without the other. A pad called the disc sits between the jaw's knob (the condyle) and the skull. It is tough fibrous tissue that acts like an extra bone. Its middle is thin and has no blood vessels or nerves, and that's where the condyle normally sits; the front edge is thicker and the back edge thickest. It is also thicker toward the inside, so if it slips off, it tends to go forward or inward. Don't call it a meniscus; that's the crescent-shaped pad in the knee. The disc splits the joint into two spaces. The jaw hinges in the lower space (condyle against disc) and slides in the upper space (disc against skull), so the disc always stays on top of the condyle. Behind the disc is tissue full of blood vessels and nerves; pressing on it hurts. Its upper layer is stretchy and pulls the disc back. The upper part of the lateral pterygoid muscle attaches to the front of the disc. The joint carries real force: you push against it every time you bite something hard. Ligaments stop movement The capsule wraps the joint and keeps the condyle from dropping out. Two small ligaments tie the disc to the inner and outer sides of the condyle; when they stretch or tear, the joint clicks (about half of people click, and ligaments don't heal). The stylomandibular and sphenomandibular ligaments limit opening and moving forward. The temporomandibular ligament has an outer slanted part that limits how far you can hinge open, and an inner flat part that stops the jaw being pushed back (like from a punch to the chin). If a patient can't close after a long appointment because the condyle slid past the bump, press down on the back of the lower jaw, never back. How muscles work Muscles can only pull. They always work in pairs, one pulling while its partner controls the motion. Parts of one muscle can fire separately, so one muscle can do several jobs. A muscle's shape and direction tell you its job. The four chewing muscles The masseter runs from the cheekbone to the angle of the jaw. It is the main power closer. Its outer part closes and pushes slightly forward; its deep part closes and pulls back. Because it pulls up and forward, it seats the joints. The temporalis fans from the side of the head to the thin coronoid process. It is mostly a fast positioner, not a power closer. Its front fibers close, middle fibers close and pull back a bit, and back fibers pull the jaw back. The cheekbone arch protects where it attaches. The lateral pterygoid is really two muscles. The lower part pulls the condyle forward, down and inward: both sides together push the jaw forward and help open; one side alone swings the chin to the other side. The upper part works when you close, holding the disc in place. The medial pterygoid runs inside the jaw angle and closes the jaw. With the masseter outside, it forms a strong sling. The exam chart Dr. Givan will use this chart for "which muscle does which movement": closing: temporalis, masseter, medial pterygoid. Opening: the lower lateral pterygoid plus the muscles above and below the hyoid. Forward: the lower lateral pterygoid plus the outer masseter. Back: the back of the temporalis plus the deep masseter. To the right: the right temporalis and right masseter, plus the left lateral and left medial pterygoids (to the left, swap sides). Opening and the hyoid The hyoid is a floating bone in the neck that touches no other bone. Muscles above it (digastric, geniohyoid, mylohyoid, stylohyoid) help open the jaw. Muscles below it (sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid) hold the hyoid still so the upper group has something to pull against. The digastric is a key opener; the mylohyoid is the floor of the mouth. The big neck muscles (sternocleidomastoid and trapezius) hold the head up.
